PASSO 1: o «pretérito perfecto» fala de: STEP 1: the «pretérito perfecto» talks about something that has already happened within a period that hasn't ended yet: today, this week, this month, this year; or something that still matters right now: «Ya he comido» (I've already eaten). STEP 2: build it in two parts: «haber» in the present + the past participle. The forms of «haber» are: he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han. STEP 3: the past participle of -ar verbs ends in «-ado»: hablar → hablado, trabajar → trabajado. -er and -ir verbs end in «-ido»: comer → comido, vivir → vivido. STEP 4: the participle never changes — it has no gender and no number. You say «Ella ha comido» and «Ellas han comido»; only «haber» changes. STEP 5: nothing ever comes between «haber» and the participle. Negation and pronouns go before «haber»: «No he comido», «Me he levantado», «Ya me he duchado». The adverb «ya» goes either before «he» or after the participle: «Ya he comido» or «He comido ya», never «He ya comido». STEP 6: the most common markers are: «hoy, esta mañana, esta tarde, esta semana, este mes, este año, ya, todavía no, alguna vez, nunca, siempre». STEP 7: the most important thing to watch: English «I have eaten» can mean either a completed action in an unfinished period (which matches Spanish «he comido» closely) or an ongoing habit, and it never changes form for that difference — Spanish «he comido» is always the first kind, a single completed action: it means «I ate (today)» or «I've already eaten», never a recurring habit. Never use «tener» in place of «haber» to build this tense: «tengo comido» is not the pretérito perfecto. STEP 8: in Spain the pretérito perfecto is used for what happened today; in much of Latin America, the pretérito indefinido (which you'll see at A2) is preferred even for today: «Hoy comí».
o «pretérito perfeito composto» do portu: English «I have eaten» and Spanish «he comido» line up closely for a single completed action within a period that hasn't ended («I've eaten already» ↔ «ya he comido»), so that part transfers well. Where it gets tricky is that English «I have eaten» can also describe a repeated habit over time («I have eaten here for years»), a sense the Spanish pretérito perfecto never carries — Spanish always treats «he comido» as one finished event, equivalent to «I ate» or «I've already eaten», and nothing more.

PASSO 1: alguns verbos muito usados têm: STEP 1: a handful of very common verbs have an irregular participle. There aren't many, and you already know most of them from their infinitive. STEP 2: learn these first: hacer → hecho, decir → dicho, ver → visto, poner → puesto, escribir → escrito, abrir → abierto, volver → vuelto, romper → roto. STEP 3: compound verbs follow their base verb: «deshacer» → deshecho; «describir» → descrito; «devolver» → devuelto. STEP 4: verbs that are irregular in the present often have a perfectly regular participle: ir → ido, ser → sido, estar → estado, tener → tenido, dar → dado, saber → sabido, querer → querido, poder → podido, salir → salido, venir → venido. STEP 5: -er and -ir verbs whose stem ends in a vowel carry an accent on the «í» of the participle: leer → leído, creer → creído, oír → oído, traer → traído, caer → caído. STEP 6: an irregular participle is used exactly the same way: «Hoy he hecho la compra» (today I did the shopping), «Hemos visto una película» (we've watched a movie), «Han escrito un correo» (they've written an email). STEP 7: to practice, answer the question «¿Qué has hecho hoy?» always with «he + participle». STEP 8: in negative sentences with «todavía no», the participle stays exactly the same: «Todavía no he visto la película».
o português também tem particípios irreg: English irregular past participles (seen, done, written, opened) are just as unpredictable as Spanish ones, so the habit of simply memorizing the irregular list transfers directly. The trap here is specific to Spanish: inventing a regular-looking form by false analogy with the infinitive — something like «he hacido» or «he escribido» — which isn't a mistake English speakers would make the same way, since English doesn't build its irregular participles off a predictable suffix pattern to begin with.

PASSO 1: para perguntar sobre uma experi: STEP 1: to ask about a life experience, use «alguna vez»: «¿Has estado alguna vez en Madrid?» (have you ever been to Madrid?). STEP 2: possible answers: «Sí, he estado una vez / dos veces / muchas veces» (yes, I've been once / twice / many times) and «No, nunca he estado» or «No he estado nunca» (no, I've never been). STEP 3: to ask whether something has already happened: «¿Has comido ya?» (have you eaten yet?). Answers: «Sí, ya he comido» or «Todavía no he comido». STEP 4: to ask about today: «¿Qué has hecho hoy?» (what have you done today?). Answers with «he + participle». STEP 5: with «usted»: «¿Ha estado alguna vez en Brasil?»; with «vosotros» (Spain): «¿Habéis estado alguna vez en Brasil?». STEP 6: false friend: «asistir a» means to attend an event (a class, a concert, a meeting) — it has nothing to do with watching a movie: a movie is something you «ve» (see/watch). STEP 7: «perder» means to lose (something, the train, your keys) and follows the same pattern: «He perdido el tren» (I missed the train). Watch out: «perder» changes e → ie in the present (pierdo).
o português «já fui a Madri» corresponde: Spanish «asistir a» looks like it should mean «to assist» or even «to watch», but it actually means «to attend» an event — a class, a concert, a meeting. The verb for watching a movie is simply «ver», the same verb used for seeing anything. The resemblance between «asistir» and English «assist» is the trap here, since the two words don't share that meaning at all.
